related_questions.question: What are the five warning signs of breast cancer?
related_questions.title: Some warning signs of breast cancer are:
list: New lump in the breast or underarm (armpit).
Thickening or swelling of part of the breast.
Irritation or dimpling of breast skin.
Redness or flaky skin in the nipple area or the breast.
Pulling in of the nipple or pain in the nipple area.

related_questions.question: What does stage 1 breast cancer feel like?
related_questions.snippet: Stage 1 breast cancer may present with symptoms or not. If symptoms are present, Stage 1 signs of breast cancer may include: A lump in the breast (this is the most common Stage 1 symptom) Nipple discharge, including bloody or clear fluid.

related_questions.question: What happens to your body when you have breast cancer?
related_questions.snippet: Cancer cells can spread into nearby breast tissue (invasion). This creates tumours that cause lumps or thickening. Invasive cancers can spread to nearby lymph nodes or other organs (metastasize). Metastasis can be life-threatening and fatal.

text_blocks.snippet: Breast cancer symptoms can vary, but common signs include a new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm, changes in breast size or shape, skin irritation or dimpling, nipple changes (like inversion or discharge), and breast pain. Early detection is crucial, as some breast cancers may not initially cause noticeable symptoms.
snippet_highlighted_words: a new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm, changes in breast size or shape, skin irritation or dimpling, nipple changes (like inversion or discharge), and breast pain

list.snippet: New lump or mass: A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area that feels different from the surrounding tissue.
Breast shape or size changes: Noticeable changes in the size or shape of one or both breasts.
Skin changes: Dimpling, puckering, redness, or scaling of the skin on the breast.
Nipple changes: Nipple retraction (turning inward), discharge (other than breast milk), or changes in nipple appearance.
Breast pain: Persistent or unusual breast pain, including a burning sensation.
Swelling: Swelling of all or part of the breast, even if no lump is felt.
Inflammatory breast cancer: A rare type that can cause a warm, red, swollen breast with skin dimpling, resembling an infection.
Advanced breast cancer: Bone pain, headaches, dizziness, chest pain, or other symptoms if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body.
Any new or unusual breast changes should be evaluated by a healthcare professional, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Don't wait for your next scheduled mammogram if you notice a change.
Even if a recent mammogram was clear, report any new changes to your doctor.
